story: Dancehall began in the late 1970s among working-class people in inner-city Kingston who could not go to dances uptown. As Edward Seaga's government replaced Michael Manley's, music moved away from internationally oriented roots reggae toward local listeners. Radio would not play it, so it spread through sound systems and record dealers. Deejays toasted over rhythm tracks from 1960s and 1970s reggae. Sound systems such as Killimanjaro and Black Scorpio brought new deejays such as General Echo and Yellowman, whose sexually explicit lyrics were called "slackness". Deejay records now mattered more than records by singers. In 1984 Wayne Smith and Noel Davey built a riddim on the "rock" preset of a Casiotone MT-40 keyboard, because Davey could not afford a Yamaha DX-7. King Jammy released it as "Under Mi Sleng Teng" in 1985, and many artists recorded over the same riddim. Afterwards most riddims were made by keyboard players alone. Shabba Ranks won a Grammy for his 1991 album As Raw as Ever, and dancehall's faster electronic beat shaped Reggae en Español.

disagreements: Start date: our record says 1980; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancehall?action=raw says it "originated in the late 1970s" and "began in the late 1970s among lower and working-class people".

Sound: our record describes 'digital-era riddims'; the article says early dancehall used rhythm tracks that "came from earlier reggae songs from the 1960s and 1970s", and the digital turn came with "Under Mi Sleng Teng" in 1985. The record's description fits from 1985, not from 1980.

Between sources (not our record): the Dancehall article says the Sleng Teng rhythm "was used in over 200 subsequent recordings"; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Mi_Sleng_Teng?action=raw says "having been used in more than 500 songs". The story gives no number.
